## References

1. [APIGen-MT: Agentic Pipeline for Multi-Turn Data Generation via Simulated Agent-Human Interplay](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03601)

# Notes

## The problem: agents fail at conversations, and nobody has the data to fix that

A customer-service agent has to do three things at once. It has to talk with a person who reveals what they want a piece at a time, it has to call APIs (look up a user, cancel an order, exchange an item) with exactly the right arguments, and it has to obey business rules (you cannot return an order that has not been delivered). Benchmarks like [[2406.12045 - Tau-Bench (Tool-Agent-User Interaction)]] showed that even frontier models fail at this combination, and fail inconsistently.

The Salesforce authors argue the bottleneck is model capability, and that the capability is missing because the training data is missing. Public pretraining text contains almost no records of "a user talks to an agent, the agent calls tools, the database changes, the user follows up". Collecting such records by hand is slow and expensive, especially when the records have to respect domain policies. Their earlier work, APIGen, generated single-turn function-calling data (one question, one tool call). APIGen-MT ("multi-turn") extends that to full conversations.

The obvious approach is to ask a strong LLM to write a whole conversation in one shot. The paper names two reasons this breaks. First, one hallucinated step anywhere in a long conversation ruins the whole sample. Second, each turn depends on the outputs of earlier tool calls, so the model has to keep a web of dependencies consistent that it cannot actually check. You end up with conversations that read well but whose tool calls would not execute, or would execute and violate policy.

## The core idea: write the answer key first, then act out the conversation

APIGen-MT splits generation into two phases.

Phase 1 writes a "blueprint" for a task. A blueprint is a triple: a user instruction q (what the user wants, written in plain language, with persona details), the groundtruth actions a_gt (the exact sequence of state-changing API calls that solves it), and the expected outputs o_gt (facts the agent must tell the user, like a refund amount). Because the blueprint has no dialogue in it, it is short enough to check thoroughly: you can run the actions against the real environment and see what they do.

Phase 2 turns a verified blueprint into a conversation. One LLM plays the human, sees only q, and reveals it gradually. Another LLM (gpt-4o in function-calling mode) plays the agent, sees only what the human says plus tool outputs, and has to figure out what to do. At the end, the environment's final state is compared against the state that a_gt produces, and the agent's messages are checked for o_gt. Only conversations that match are kept.

The clever part is that the answer key is written before the exam is taken. The conversation is free to be messy and natural (the agent can call extra read APIs, ask clarifying questions, go in a different order), but it is graded against something verified. This is the same move as [[single-call-trajectory-synthesis]] and TaskCraft ([[2506.10055 - TaskCraft Automated Generation of Agentic Tasks]]): make the verifiable object first, and let the expensive, noisy part be graded against it.

## The formal frame: a POMDP with two kinds of observation

The paper writes the interaction as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process, meaning the agent acts without seeing the full state of the world. The tuple is (U, S, A, O, T, R):

- U is the space of user intents; the hidden q the human is trying to accomplish lives here.
- S is the state: the environment's database plus the conversation history.
- A = {tool_call, response}. The agent at each turn either calls a tool or says something to the human.
- O = O_E ∪ O_H. Observations come from two sources: the environment (a JSON tool result) or the human (their next message).
- T is the transition. A tool call moves the environment state s_E^t to s_E^{t+1} and returns o_E. A response moves the human's state s_H^t to s_H^{t+1} and returns o_H.
- R(ΔS_E, a) is the reward. ΔS_E is the cumulative change to the database over the episode; a is the sequence of messages the agent sent the human.

Two details matter. The environment state is latent to both parties: the human cannot see the database, and the agent only sees slices of it through tool outputs. And the reward is computed on outcomes, not on the path. The agent is scored on what changed in the database and what it said, not on which sequence of calls it made. In τ-bench's convention this is binary: r = 1 if the final database equals the database produced by a_gt and every item in o_gt appears in the agent's responses, else r = 0. That outcome-only reward is what lets Phase 2 accept many different conversations for the same blueprint.

## Phase 1 in detail: generating a blueprint that is actually correct

The paper instantiates everything on τ-bench's two domains, Retail and Airline, which ship with Python-implemented APIs (15 "read" and 13 "write" across both), a mock database, and written policy documents.

### Building the prompt: API graph plus five samplers

The generator LLM needs context to propose a realistic task. The authors build that context by sampling.

The API dependency graph comes first. Each API is a node. There is an edge from API A to API B when B's inputs can come from A's outputs and the pair is allowed under domain policy. Random walks through this graph give plausible call sequences, for example find_user → get_order_details → exchange_items, rather than random combinations.

Five samplers then fill the prompt:

1. API sampler. It separates read APIs (look things up) from write APIs (change the database). The blueprint's a_gt focuses on write calls. This is a deliberate non-default choice: the groundtruth does not prescribe which lookups the agent should do, only which changes must happen. That leaves the Phase 2 agent free to explore with reads, and it matches the outcome-only reward.
2. Policy sampler. It pulls relevant rules from the domain policy. More write calls combined with more policy constraints means a harder task.
3. Domain data sampler. It pulls real user and order records (with metadata like price and attributes) so the task refers to things that exist, without dumping the full database into context.
4. Persona sampler. It pulls personality descriptions from PersonaHub so users differ in tone and situation.
5. Example sampler. It pulls few-shot examples of well-formed tasks for the sampled APIs.

Sampling frequencies are randomized per iteration to avoid repetitive tasks. The generator outputs four tagged fields: a thought, the instruction q, the actions a_gt, and the outputs o_gt. The prompt (Figure 8) tells it to only make tool calls that modify the database, and to answer information requests by reading the provided user data directly into o_gt.

### Three-stage validation

Stage 1, action validation, is rule-based and has three checks.

- Format check: all four tagged fields exist, tool calls are valid JSON, outputs are strings.
- Execution check: each action in a_gt is actually run in the τ-bench environment. Wrong API names, wrong argument names, or wrong types fail here. The cumulative database change is recorded as a diff_patch, like a git diff of the database.
- Policy compliance check: the authors translated domain policies into Python unit tests that run on the execution trace. This catches violations that only appear from combinations of actions, for example action B being invalid because action A already changed the state.

Stage 2, alignment validation, is semantic. A committee of different LLMs each reads q, a_gt, o_gt, the tool descriptions and the diff_patch, and scores four binary criteria (Figure 9): Correctness (do the actions implement the instruction), Completeness (is the instruction detailed enough and fully addressed), Satisfaction (do the outputs answer the user's information requests), and Creativity (is it a non-trivial, plausible scenario). Majority voting across the committee decides each criterion. The point of the diff_patch here is important: the judges do not have to simulate the API calls in their heads. They see the concrete effect on the database and can ask "is this exactly what the user asked for, with nothing extra?"

Stage 3, final semantic review. Tasks whose aggregated average score clears a threshold are accepted. Failing tasks go to a feedback generator (Figure 10), which reads all the judges' reviews, summarizes points of agreement, and writes actionable feedback. The generator then revises the task, a reflection loop. The maximum number of feedback rounds is 3 for Retail and 5 for Airline.

The committee idea connects to [[llm-as-judge-evaluation-methodology]] and [[2306.05685 - Judging LLM-as-a-Judge (MT-Bench)]]: single judges are biased and noisy, so average several. The committee here is gpt-4o and DeepSeek V3 style models; [[correlated-frontier-monitors-limit-ensembling]] is the caveat that voting only helps if judges make different errors.

### How much the loop helps

The headline Phase 1 number is that the feedback loop raises the task acceptance rate from 28% to 70%, a 2.5x gain. Put plainly: without reflection, most generated blueprints are thrown away; with it, most are rescued. This is a cost number more than a quality number. It says the pipeline wastes less generation, not that accepted tasks are better.

### Reverse Task Recombination: building hard tasks from easy verified ones

Long tasks with many write calls are hard to generate directly, because one subtle policy conflict fails the whole thing. The fix borrows from modular software design.

1. Take several simple tasks T1, T2, ... that already passed all validation and share the same user persona.
2. Concatenate their actions (a_combined = a_gt,1 ∘ a_gt,2 ∘ ...) and merge their outputs (o_combined = o_gt,1 ⊕ o_gt,2 ⊕ ...). Here ∘ means "append the action sequence" and ⊕ means "collect the outputs".
3. Rerun the policy check on the combined sequence, because combining can create conflicts, such as returning and cancelling the same order.
4. Ask the LLM to write one coherent instruction q_combined that covers everything.
5. Send the combined task to Stage 2 alignment validation; Stage 1 format and execution checks are skipped.

The paper's justification for skipping Stage 1 is that each piece was already checked. My reading is that this is weaker than it sounds for the execution part. Each piece was executed from the original database state, not from the state after the earlier pieces ran. If T1 modifies an order that T2 also touches, the concatenated sequence could fail or behave differently at execution time. The policy recheck catches rule conflicts, but it is not the same as re-executing. Phase 2 will reject such tasks anyway (no conversation can reach an unreachable state), so the cost is wasted simulation, not bad data.

## Phase 2 in detail: simulated human, test agent, rejection sampling

The human LLM gets the trajectory collection prompt (Figure 11): reveal one line at a time, only give information needed for the current step, do not invent facts not in the intent, emit ###STOP### when done, paraphrase rather than repeat the intent, keep the persona. The human never sees the APIs, which mimics a real user.

The agent is gpt-4o with function calling. Each blueprint is attempted up to three times, and the union of unique successful trajectories is kept. This is rejection sampling: generate many, keep only r = 1. About 67% of simulations succeed. Surviving trajectories average about 12 turns, 7 tool calls and 6 user turns, with the longest at 29 turns.

### Stabilizing the simulated human

A human simulator drifts. Over many turns it forgets details, changes an order number, or gets talked into something by the agent. That noise corrupts both data collection and evaluation (see [[llm-user-simulator-design-and-auditing]]). The fix is Best-of-N with self-critique: for each human turn, sample N = 4 candidate messages, score each with a judge prompt (Figure 12) from 0 to 10, and send the best one. The judge prompt gives full marks when specific item, order, or personal details match the task description, lower scores for changed details, and low scores for unhelpful replies like "I don't remember". Normal conversation, clarifying questions and ###STOP### count as correct.

This is a simple, general trick worth remembering: you do not need a better user model, just a filter on its outputs that checks them against the ground truth it was given.

## Training: filtered behavioral cloning

Behavioral cloning means supervised imitation of demonstrations. "Filtered" means the demonstrations were kept only if they succeeded. Each trajectory is split at every assistant turn, and the model is trained to predict only the assistant's tokens; user messages, tool outputs and the system prompt are masked out of the loss. Written out:

L(θ) = − Σ_{τ : r(τ)=1} Σ_{t ∈ assistant turns of τ} Σ_i log π_θ(y_{t,i} | h_t, y_{t,<i})

- τ is a trajectory; the outer sum only runs over trajectories whose reward r(τ) was 1.
- t indexes the assistant turns; h_t is everything that came before that turn (system prompt, user messages, previous assistant turns, tool outputs).
- y_{t,i} is the i-th token of the assistant's turn t, which may be a tool call or a message.
- π_θ is the model being trained.

The masking matters because the model should learn to act as the agent, not to imitate the simulated user or predict JSON tool outputs.

Base models are Llama 3.1/3.2 Instruct and Qwen 2.5 Instruct from 1B to 70B, full fine-tuning with LLaMA-Factory, DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, FlashAttention 2, bf16, AdamW, at most 3 epochs on one H200 node. The resulting family is xLAM-2-fc-r.

One detail to not miss: APIGen-MT data is not the only training data. The models are jointly trained with single-turn function-calling data from the original APIGen and other agentic data. The paper gives no ablation separating the contribution of APIGen-MT trajectories from this mixture, and it does not state the total training set size beyond the 5K released subset.

## Results

### BFCL v3 (Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard)

BFCL scores single-turn calls (is the call syntactically and semantically right), multi-turn function calling, and hallucination (relevance: call a tool when one applies; irrelevance: refrain when none does). xLAM-2-70b-fc-r ranks first overall at 78.19% and xLAM-2-32b-fc-r second at 75.83%, as of April 2025.

The overall rank hides where the gain comes from. On single-turn categories xLAM-2 is roughly level with or slightly below GPT-4o. The gap is in multi-turn: 75.12% for the 70B, 69.25% for the 8B, even 43.12% for the 1B, against 41% for GPT-4o (FC) and 36% for o1. A 1B model beating o1 on multi-turn function calling is the most surprising number in the paper, and it points to multi-turn skill being a data problem rather than a scale problem.

A non-monotone detail: on Relevance, the 70B scores 66.67 while the 32B, 8B and 3B score 83.33, 83.33 and 94.44. Bigger was not better on knowing when to call a tool.

### τ-bench

τ-bench scores pass@1 success with a simulated user on Retail and Airline. xLAM-2-70b-fc-r gets 67.1 Retail, 45.2 Airline, 56.2 overall, above GPT-4o (52.9) and the Llama 3.1 70B base (38.2), below Claude 3.5 Sonnet (new) (60.1) and o1 (63.9), and well below Claude 3.7 Sonnet with an optimized prompt (69.8). The 8B at 46.7 beats the 70B Llama base.

Two things are worth being honest about.

First, the training data was generated inside τ-bench's own environment: its APIs, its policies, its mock database, its users and orders. The evaluation is the τ-bench test set on the same domains. This is in-domain training, closer to "train on the environment, test on held-out tasks in that environment" than to generalization. BFCL is the out-of-environment check, and the gains there are concentrated in multi-turn, which is consistent with genuine skill transfer, but τ-bench numbers should be read as in-distribution.

Second, the student beats the teacher. The Phase 2 agent that produced every trajectory was gpt-4o, which scores 52.9 overall; the 70B student scores 56.2, and 67.1 vs 62.8 on Retail. Rejection sampling explains this: the student only imitates the teacher's successes, so it learns a filtered policy the teacher does not reliably follow.

A small inconsistency: Figure 1 lists Llama 3.1 70B at 20.6 on Airline while Table 2 gives 26.0.

### Consistency: pass^k

pass^k, from τ-bench, is the probability that all k independent trials of the same task succeed, averaged over tasks. If a task succeeded c times out of n trials, the unbiased estimate is C(c, k) / C(n, k), where C is "n choose k". pass^1 is ordinary success rate; pass^k falls as k grows unless the model is reliable. The xLAM-2 curves fall less steeply, and on Airline the 70B's pass^5 exceeds Claude 3.5 Sonnet (new) even though its pass^1 is lower. For deployment this is arguably the more important number: a support agent that works 60% of the time on every task beats one that works 100% on some and 0% on others unpredictably. See [[multi-run-consistency-testing-for-llm-agents]].

### The BoN user makes evaluation more stable, and scores go up

Table 3 runs 5 trials on Retail. GPT-4o goes from 62.8 average with variance 11.1 (naive user) to 67.0 with variance 2.6 (BoN user). xLAM-2-70b goes from 67.1 / 9.7 to 68.8 / 4.0. Note what this implies: part of what τ-bench measures as agent failure is actually user-simulator failure. A noisier user lowers scores and makes them less reproducible. Anyone comparing τ-bench numbers across papers should ask which user simulator was used.

### Where xLAM-2 still loses

Tasks are bucketed into short (under 13 turns), medium (13 to 18) and long (over 18) by how many turns Claude needed. On long tasks xLAM-2-70b is well ahead of GPT-4o but behind Claude. It also needs more user interactions than Claude, which the authors attribute to it retrieving user details in stages. That is plausibly inherited from the teacher: gpt-4o's style of asking for information piecemeal is exactly what was cloned.

## Limitations the paper states, and ones it does not

Stated: the BoN user reduces but does not remove simulation noise; failed Phase 2 trajectories are thrown away though they could serve as contrastive or negative signal; multi-stage validation is computationally expensive; only two domains were tried; RL-based self-improvement is left to future work. The failed-trajectory point connects directly to the RL follow-ups in the vault, [[2504.20073 - RAGEN StarPO Multi-Turn Agent RL]] and [[2505.10978 - GiGPO Group-in-Group Policy Optimization for LLM Agent Training]], which use failures as learning signal instead of discarding them.

Not stated but visible in the setup:

- No ablations on what drives the gains. There is no model trained without Reverse Task Recombination, without the committee, or without the mixed-in APIGen single-turn data, so the paper shows the pipeline works but not which parts matter.
- The pipeline needs an executable environment with written policies and a database. τ-bench provides all three. Porting to a new domain means building those first, which is the hard part; [[2511.01824 - Simia Simulating Environments with Reasoning Models for Agent Training]] attacks exactly this by simulating the environment instead.
- Data diversity is bounded by the teacher. Every successful trajectory is something gpt-4o could already do at least once in three tries; the student cannot learn behaviors the teacher never produced.
- Policy compliance depends on hand-translating policies into unit tests, which is manual work per domain and only as complete as the tests.

## How it fits with other work in the vault

- [[2406.12045 - Tau-Bench (Tool-Agent-User Interaction)]] provides the environment, the reward, the user-simulation setup and pass^k. APIGen-MT is essentially a training-data factory built on τ-bench's machinery.
- [[2504.21798 - SWE-smith Scaling Data for SWE Agents]] and [[2506.10055 - TaskCraft Automated Generation of Agentic Tasks]] follow the same pattern for other domains: synthesize verifiable tasks, run a strong agent, keep the successes, clone.
- [[llm-user-simulator-design-and-auditing]]: the BoN self-critique user is a concrete, cheap simulator-hardening technique.
- [[2504.13958 - ToolRL Reward Design for Tool-Integrated Reasoning]] is the RL alternative to filtered BC for tool use.

## Key claims

1. The reflection-based feedback loop in Phase 1 raises the fraction of generated blueprints that pass validation from 28% to 70%. Setup: τ-bench Retail and Airline, gpt-4o and DeepSeek V3 as generator and judges, up to 3 (Retail) or 5 (Airline) feedback rounds.
> Our agentic pipeline involving review committee and iterative refinement via reflection provides a 2.5x boost to the task collection success rate to attain 70%.
(Section 4.3, Statistics; Figure 4)

2. Collected trajectories are long, averaging about 12 turns for gpt-4o to finish. Setup: Phase 2 simulations with gpt-4o as agent, about 67% simulation success, averages of 7 tool calls and 6 user turns.
> Figure 5 shows that we can efficiently collect long trajectories requiring a strong model like gpt-4o to take an average 12 turns to complete the task using APIGen-MT.
(Section 4.3, Statistics)

3. xLAM-2-70b-fc-r and xLAM-2-32b-fc-r took first and second place on BFCL v3 overall, at 78.19% and 75.83%. Setup: BFCL v3 leaderboard snapshot of 04/03/2025, function-calling mode.
> xLAM-2-70b-fc-r and xLAM-2-32b-fc-r achieve the top 2 positions on the leaderboard with overall accuracies of 78.19% and 75.83% respectively, surpassing all proprietary and open-source models.
(Section 5.2, BFCL v3 Results; Table 1)

4. The gain is concentrated in multi-turn function calling, where even the 1B model (43.12%) beats o1 (36%) and GPT-4o in FC mode (41%). Setup: BFCL v3 multi-turn category.
> xLAM-2-3b-fc-r at 56.00%, and even xLAM-2-1b-fc-r at 43.12% - all substantially outperforming o1 (36%) and gpt-4o in function-calling mode (41%).
(Section 5.2, BFCL v3 Results; Table 1)

5. On τ-bench the 70B model reaches 56.2% average pass@1, above GPT-4o (52.9%), the agent that generated its training data. Setup: τ-bench Retail + Airline, naive user, averaged over at least 5 trials, only the benchmark's think tool, no prompt optimization; training data generated in the same τ-bench domains.
> Our xLAM-2-70b-fc-r model achieves a 56.2% success rate, outperforming Llama 3.1 70B Instruct (38.2%), DeepSeek v3 (40.6%), and even proprietary models like GPT-4o (52.9%)
(Section 5.2, τ-bench Results; Table 2)

6. Smaller xLAM-2 models beat larger untuned baselines on τ-bench: 32B at 54.6% and 8B at 46.7% versus Llama 3.1 70B Instruct at 38.2%. Setup: same as claim 5.
> Notably, our smaller variants like xLAM-2-32b-fc-r (54.6%) and xLAM-2-8b-fc-r (46.7%) surpass larger baselines
(Section 5.2, τ-bench Results)

7. xLAM-2-70b is more consistent across repeated trials than Claude 3.5 Sonnet (new) on Airline: higher pass^5 despite lower pass^1. Setup: τ-bench, naive user, 5 trials per task.
> Notably on the more complex airline domain, xLAM-2-70b-fc-r has higher passˆ5 score than Claude, despite having a slightly lower passˆ1 suggesting higher reliability and consistency across multiple trials.
(Section 5.3; Figure 6)

8. The Best-of-N self-critiquing user simulator raises agent success and cuts variance across trials, for example GPT-4o goes from 62.8% (variance 11.1) to 67.0% (variance 2.6). Setup: τ-bench Retail, 5 trials, N = 4 candidate user messages scored 0 to 10 by a judge prompt.
> The average success rate is higher with lower variance using BoN based user simulation, indicative of a more stable evaluation.
(Section 5.3; Table 3 caption)

9. xLAM-2-70b needs more user interactions than Claude to finish a task, which the authors put down to it gathering user details in stages. Setup: τ-bench, tasks bucketed by Claude's turn count across 8 trials.
> The plot reveals that xLAM-2-70b-fc-r is at par with gpt-4o but requires more interactions compared to Claude, which can be attributed to its method of retrieving user details in stages, necessitating more turns.
(Section 5.4; Figure 7)

10. Complex tasks can be built by joining verified simple tasks and re-validating only the semantics and policy of the combination. No number; there is no ablation of this component.
> This method allows for the scalable generation of complex, multi-step tasks with greater reliability, as it builds upon verified components while focusing the validation effort on the semantic coherence and alignment of the combined whole.
(Section 4.1.3)
